use std::hash::{Hash, Hasher};
use std::collections::hash_map::DefaultHasher;

struct MyHashMap<K, V> {
    buckets: Vec<Vec<(K, V)>>,
    size: usize,
}
impl<K: Hash + Eq, V> MyHashMap<K, V> {
    fn insert(&mut self, key: K, value: V) {
        let mut hasher = DefaultHasher::new();
        key.hash(&mut hasher);
        let hash = hasher.finish() as usize % self.buckets.len();
        self.buckets[hash].push((key, value));
    }

lessons.title: Graphs & BFS/DFS
lessons.html:
Graph Algorithms

Breadth-first and depth-first traversal with applications.

Adjacency List:

use std::collections::{HashMap, VecDeque, HashSet};

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
struct Graph<T> {
    adj: HashMap<T, Vec<T>>,
}
impl<T: Eq + Hash + Clone> Graph<T> {
    fn bfs(&self, start: &T) -> Vec<T> {
        let mut visited = HashSet::new();
        let mut queue = VecDeque::new();
        queue.push_back(start.clone());
        
        while let Some(node) = queue.pop_front() {
            if !visited.insert(node.clone()) { continue; }
            for neighbor in self.adj.get(&node).unwrap() {
                queue.push_back(neighbor.clone());
            }
        }
        visited.into_iter().collect()
    }
}

Optimize with Memoization

Solve complex problems by breaking into subproblems.

Fibonacci DP:

fn fib_memo(n: usize, memo: &mut HashMap<usize, u64>) -> u64 {
    if let Some(&result) = memo.get(&n) {
        return result;
    }
    
    let result = if n <= 1 { n as u64 } else {
        fib_memo(n - 1, memo) + fib_memo(n - 2, memo)
    };
    
    memo.insert(n, result);
    result
}

Binary Heaps Implementation

O(log n) insert and extract-min operations.

Min-Heap:

struct MinHeap<T> {
    heap: Vec<T>,
}
impl<T: PartialOrd> MinHeap<T> {
    fn heapify_up(&mut self, idx: usize) {
        let mut child = idx;
        while child > 0 {
            let parent = (child - 1) / 2;
            if self.heap[child] < self.heap[parent] {
                self.heap.swap(child, parent);
                child = parent;
            } else { break; }
        }
    }
}

lessons.title: Red-Black Trees
lessons.html:
Self-Balancing BST

Red-Black trees guarantee O(log n) operations through color properties and rotations. Used in Rust's BTreeMap.

Node Structure:

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]
enum Color { Red, Black }

struct RBNode<T: Ord> {
    value: T,
    color: Color,
    left: Option<Box<RBNode<T>>>,
    right: Option<Box<RBNode<T>>>,
}

Insert with Fixup:

impl<T: Ord> RBNode<T> {
    fn insert(&mut self, value: T) {
        if value < self.value {
            if let Some(ref mut left) = self.left { left.insert(value); }
            else { self.left = Some(Box::new(RBNode::new(value))); }
        } else if value > self.value {
            if let Some(ref mut right) = self.right { right.insert(value); }
            else { self.right = Some(Box::new(RBNode::new(value))); }
        }
        self.fixup();
    }

    fn fixup(&mut self) {
        if Self::is_red(&self.right) && !Self::is_red(&self.left) {
            self.rotate_left();
        }
        if Self::is_red(&self.left) && Self::is_red(&self.left.as_ref().unwrap().left) {
            self.rotate_right();
        }
        if Self::is_red(&self.left) && Self::is_red(&self.right) {
            self.flip_colors();
        }
    }
}

  2. Compare performance with Rust's BTreeMap
  3. Add visualization of tree rotations

Key Takeaways:

  • Red-Black trees maintain balance through color rules
  • Rotations preserve BST property while rebalancing
  • Left-leaning RB trees simplify implementation

lessons.title: Graph Shortest Path - Dijkstra & A*
lessons.html:
Pathfinding Algorithms

Shortest path algorithms are essential for GPS navigation, network routing, and game AI.

Dijkstra's Algorithm:

use std::collections::{HashMap, BinaryHeap};

#[derive(Eq, PartialEq)]
struct State { cost: u32, node: usize }

impl Ord for State {
    fn cmp(&self, other: &Self) -> std::cmp::Ordering {
        other.cost.cmp(&self.cost)  // Min-heap
    }
}

fn dijkstra(adj: &[Vec<(usize, u32)>], start: usize, end: usize) -> Option<u32> {
    let n = adj.len();
    let mut dist = vec![u32::MAX; n];
    let mut heap = BinaryHeap::new();

    dist[start] = 0;
    heap.push(State { cost: 0, node: start });

    while let Some(State { cost, node }) = heap.pop() {
        if node == end { return Some(cost); }
        if cost > dist[node] { continue; }
        for &(to, weight) in &adj[node] {
            let next = cost + weight;
            if next < dist[to] {
                dist[to] = next;
                heap.push(State { cost: next, node: to });
            }
        }
    }
    None
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement A* with a heuristic function
  2. Find the shortest path in a 2D grid with obstacles
  3. Use Dijkstra for network routing optimization

Key Takeaways:

  • Dijkstra finds shortest paths in weighted graphs
  • BinaryHeap provides efficient min-extraction
  • A* with a good heuristic is faster than Dijkstra

lessons.title: Disjoint Set Union (Union-Find)
lessons.html:
DSU with Path Compression

DSU tracks partitions of elements. Near O(1) operations with path compression and union by rank.

Implementation:

struct DSU {
    parent: Vec<usize>,
    rank: Vec<usize>,
    size: Vec<usize>,
}

impl DSU {
    fn new(n: usize) -> Self {
        DSU { parent: (0..n).collect(), rank: vec![0; n], size: vec![1; n] }
    }

    fn find(&mut self, x: usize) -> usize {
        if self.parent[x] != x {
            self.parent[x] = self.find(self.parent[x]);
        }
        self.parent[x]
    }

    fn union(&mut self, x: usize, y: usize) -> bool {
        let rx = self.find(x);
        let ry = self.find(y);
        if rx == ry { return false; }
        match self.rank[rx].cmp(&self.rank[ry]) {
            Less => { self.parent[rx] = ry; self.size[ry] += self.size[rx]; }
            Greater => { self.parent[ry] = rx; self.size[rx] += self.size[ry]; }
            Equal => { self.parent[ry] = rx; self.rank[rx] += 1; self.size[rx] += self.size[ry]; }
        }
        true
    }
}

Kruskal's MST:

fn kruskal(n: usize, edges: &mut [(usize, usize, u32)]) -> u32 {
    edges.sort_by_key(|&(_, _, w)| w);
    let mut dsu = DSU::new(n);
    edges.iter().filter(|&&(u, v, _)| dsu.union(u, v)).map(|&(_, _, w)| w).sum()
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Solve the number of connected components problem
  2. Implement Kruskal's MST and test on random graphs
  3. Use DSU to detect cycles in a graph

Key Takeaways:

  • Path compression flattens the tree structure
  • Union by rank keeps trees shallow
  • Amortized time is O(alpha(n)) ~ constant

lessons.title: Segment Trees
lessons.html:
Range Query Data Structure

Segment trees answer range queries (sum, min, max) and update values in O(log n) time.

Generic Implementation:

struct SegTree<T, F> {
    n: usize,
    data: Vec<T>,
    identity: T,
    combine: F,
}

impl<T: Clone, F: Fn(&T, &T) -> T> SegTree<T, F> {
    fn new(arr: &[T], identity: T, combine: F) -> Self {
        let n = arr.len();
        let mut data = vec![identity.clone(); 2 * n];
        for (i, val) in arr.iter().enumerate() { data[n + i] = val.clone(); }
        for i in (1..n).rev() { data[i] = combine(&data[2*i], &data[2*i+1]); }
        SegTree { n, data, identity, combine }
    }

    fn query(&self, mut l: usize, mut r: usize) -> T {
        l += self.n; r += self.n;
        let mut left = self.identity.clone();
        let mut right = self.identity.clone();
        while l < r {
            if l & 1 == 1 { left = (self.combine)(&left, &self.data[l]); l += 1; }
            if r & 1 == 1 { r -= 1; right = (self.combine)(&self.data[r], &right); }
            l /= 2; r /= 2;
        }
        (self.combine)(&left, &right)
    }

    fn update(&mut self, mut idx: usize, value: T) {
        idx += self.n;
        self.data[idx] = value;
        idx /= 2;
        while idx > 0 {
            self.data[idx] = (self.combine)(&self.data[2*idx], &self.data[2*idx+1]);
            idx /= 2;
        }
    }
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement range minimum query with updates
  2. Add lazy propagation for range updates
  3. Use segment tree to solve the range sum problem

Key Takeaways:

  • Segment trees handle point updates and range queries
  • The generic design works for any associative operation
  • Memory is 2 * next_power_of_two(n)

lessons.title: String Algorithms - KMP Pattern Matching
lessons.html:
Efficient Substring Search

KMP finds patterns in O(n+m) time using the prefix function (LPS array).

KMP Implementation:

fn build_lps(pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<usize> {
    let m = pattern.len();
    let mut lps = vec![0; m];
    let mut len = 0;
    let mut i = 1;
    while i < m {
        if pattern[i] == pattern[len] {
            len += 1; lps[i] = len; i += 1;
        } else if len > 0 {
            len = lps[len - 1];
        } else {
            lps[i] = 0; i += 1;
        }
    }
    lps
}

fn kmp(text: &[u8], pattern: &[u8]) -> Vec<usize> {
    let n = text.len(); let m = pattern.len();
    if m == 0 || m > n { return vec![]; }
    let lps = build_lps(pattern);
    let mut matches = vec![];
    let mut i = 0; let mut j = 0;
    while i < n {
        if pattern[j] == text[i] { i += 1; j += 1; }
        if j == m { matches.push(i - j); j = lps[j - 1]; }
        else if i < n && pattern[j] != text[i] {
            if j > 0 { j = lps[j - 1]; } else { i += 1; }
        }
    }
    matches
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement Rabin-Karp with rolling hash
  2. Solve the find-all-anagrams-in-a-string problem
  3. Build a simple text search engine

Key Takeaways:

  • LPS array avoids backtracking in text
  • KMP runs in linear time regardless of input
  • Prefix function has many other applications

lessons.title: Advanced Bit Manipulation
lessons.html:
Bitwise Tricks & Techniques

Bit manipulation provides elegant solutions for certain problems and is critical for embedded systems.

Common Operations:

fn is_power_of_two(n: u32) -> bool {
    n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0
}

fn count_bits(mut n: u32) -> u32 {
    let mut count = 0;
    while n > 0 { n &= n - 1; count += 1; }
    count
}

fn get_bit(num: u32, pos: u32) -> bool {
    (num >> pos) & 1 == 1
}

fn set_bit(num: u32, pos: u32) -> u32 {
    num | (1 << pos)
}

fn clear_bit(num: u32, pos: u32) -> u32 {
    num & !(1 << pos)
}

fn swap(a: &mut u32, b: &mut u32) {
    *a ^= *b; *b ^= *a; *a ^= *b;
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Find the single non-repeating element in an array
  2. Implement a bit vector for a prime sieve
  3. Solve subset generation using bitmasks

Key Takeaways:

  • XOR is its own inverse for swapping and finding duplicates
  • n & (n-1) clears the lowest set bit
  • Bit operations are extremely fast (single CPU cycle)

lessons.title: Concurrency with Threads & Channels
lessons.html:
Fearless Concurrency in Rust

Rust's ownership model makes concurrent programming safe. The standard library provides threads, channels, and atomics.

Channels:

use std::sync::mpsc;
use std::thread;

let (tx, rx) = mpsc::channel();

for id in 0..4 {
    let tx = tx.clone();
    thread::spawn(move || {
        tx.send(format!("Thread {}: hello", id)).unwrap();
    });
}
drop(tx);  // Close sender

for msg in rx {
    println!("Got: {}", msg);
}

Shared State:

use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};

let counter = Arc::new(Mutex::new(0));
let mut handles = vec![];

for _ in 0..10 {
    let counter = Arc::clone(&counter);
    handles.push(thread::spawn(move || {
        *counter.lock().unwrap() += 1;
    }));
}
for h in handles { h.join().unwrap(); }
println!("Result: {}", *counter.lock().unwrap());

lessons.title: Rust Design Patterns
lessons.html:
Common Patterns in Idiomatic Rust

Rust's type system and ownership enable robust design patterns that prevent bugs at compile time.

Builder Pattern:

#[derive(Default)]
struct QueryBuilder {
    select: Option<String>,
    from: Option<String>,
    where_clause: Option<String>,
    limit: Option<usize>,
}

impl QueryBuilder {
    fn new() -> Self { Self::default() }
    fn select(mut self, cols: &str) -> Self { self.select = Some(cols.to_string()); self }
    fn from(mut self, table: &str) -> Self { self.from = Some(table.to_string()); self }
    fn where_clause(mut self, cond: &str) -> Self { self.where_clause = Some(format!("WHERE {}", cond)); self }
    fn limit(mut self, n: usize) -> Self { self.limit = Some(n); self }

    fn build(&self) -> Result<String, &'static str> {
        let select = self.select.as_deref().ok_or("SELECT required")?;
        let from = self.from.as_deref().ok_or("FROM required")?;
        let mut q = format!("SELECT {} FROM {}", select, from);
        if let Some(ref w) = self.where_clause { q.push_str(&format!(" {}", w)); }
        if let Some(l) = self.limit { q.push_str(&format!(" LIMIT {}", l)); }
        Ok(q)
    }
}

Practice Exercises:

  1. Implement the newtype pattern for type safety
  2. Use RAII for resource management
  3. Create a state machine using the type system

Key Takeaways:

  • Builder pattern creates complex objects step by step
  • Newtypes prevent logic errors at compile time
  • RAII guarantees resource cleanup
